title: Renal colic and kidney stones (urolithiasis)
subject: urology
summary: Give an NSAID first for renal colic, confirm with low-dose non-contrast CT (ultrasound in pregnancy and children), offer an alpha-blocker for distal ureteric stones 5 to 10 mm, and treat an obstructed infected kidney as an emergency needing immediate antibiotics and urgent decompression by stent or nephrostomy.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Sudden severe colicky loin pain radiating to the groin, restlessness, nausea and vomiting. Dipstick haematuria is common, but its absence does not exclude a stone.
Red flags: fever, rigors or sepsis; solitary or transplanted kidney; bilateral obstruction; anuria or rising creatinine; pregnancy; pain not controlled by analgesia.
Do not miss: leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (older patients), ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, pyelonephritis, biliary disease, bowel obstruction, testicular torsion.

sections.title: Analgesia and first steps
items: First line: an NSAID by any route (for example diclofenac 75 mg IM); NSAIDs relieve colic better than opioids. Take care with CKD, cardiovascular disease, GI bleeding risk and dehydration.
If NSAIDs are contraindicated or not enough: IV paracetamol (NICE). If both fail or are contraindicated: an opioid other than pethidine; ketamine is an alternative in the acute setting (EAU).
Do not give antispasmodics (such as hyoscine or drotaverine); they add nothing to NSAIDs (NICE).
Give an antiemetic as needed. Pain not controlled by drugs: urgent urology for decompression (stent or nephrostomy) or ureteroscopic stone removal.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Urine dipstick (blood, leucocytes, nitrite, pH), microscopy or culture; creatinine, electrolytes, calcium, uric acid, FBC and CRP; coagulation if intervention is likely; pregnancy test in women of childbearing age.
Low-dose non-contrast CT KUB within 24 hours of presentation (NICE), and immediately with fever, a solitary kidney or diagnostic doubt (EAU).
Pregnancy: ultrasound first, MRI second, low-dose CT as a last option. Children: ultrasound first, low-dose CT only if still uncertain.
Strain the urine and send any passed stone for analysis (infrared spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction) in every first-time stone former.

sections.title: Ureteric stones: observation and medical expulsive therapy
items: Small uncomplicated ureteric stones with controlled pain: observe with periodic review. About 75% of stones under 5 mm pass, taking on average about 17 days (range 6 to 29).

Offer an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily, off-label) as MET for distal ureteric stones 5 to 10 mm (EAU). AUA offers MET for distal stones 10 mm or smaller for about 30 days and may offer it for mid and proximal stones.
In patients expected to pass the stone, a regular NSAID for 3 to 10 days (for example diclofenac 100 to 150 mg a day) reduces recurrent colic.
Stop MET and refer if infection, refractory pain or declining renal function develops. Confirm passage with imaging if it is uncertain.
Uric acid (radiolucent) stones: oral alkalinisation with alkaline citrate or sodium bicarbonate to urine pH 7.0 to 7.2, combined with tamsulosin for ureteric stones.

sections.title: Emergency: obstructed infected kidney, and indications for removal
items: An obstructed kidney with signs of infection, or anuria, is a urological emergency: take blood and urine cultures, start IV antibiotics immediately (per the local antibiogram, see the Antibiogram tab) and arrange urgent decompression by ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
Send urine from the drained collecting system for culture, adjust antibiotics to results, involve ICU if septic, and delay definitive stone treatment until the infection has cleared.

Active removal is indicated for a low chance of spontaneous passage, persistent pain despite analgesia, persistent obstruction, or renal insufficiency (renal failure, bilateral obstruction or a single kidney).
Ureteroscopy gives a higher single-procedure stone-free rate; shock wave lithotripsy has lower morbidity. Kidney stones over 2 cm: percutaneous nephrolithotomy first line (AUA 2026).

sections.title: Special groups
items: Pregnancy: manage with the obstetrician; paracetamol first and NSAIDs generally avoided. Observe if symptoms are controlled; if passage fails, ureteroscopy, or a stent or nephrostomy with frequent changes (AUA 2026).
Children: ultrasound first; complete stone analysis and metabolic evaluation in every child because recurrence risk is high.
CKD, single or transplanted kidney: early imaging and urology involvement; avoid NSAIDs when GFR is reduced.
India: antispasmodics (drotaverine, hyoscine) are widely used for colic but add no benefit over NSAIDs; stones are common in hot regions, so stress fluid intake.

sections.title: Prevention of recurrence
items: All stone formers: fluid 2.5 to 3.0 L a day (water preferred) for a urine output of 2.0 to 2.5 L a day; balanced diet rich in vegetables and fibre; limit sugary drinks.
Do not restrict dietary calcium: aim for 1 to 1.2 g a day. Limit salt to 4 to 5 g a day and animal protein to 0.8 to 1.0 g/kg a day; keep a normal BMI; avoid excess vitamin C.
High-risk or recurrent stone formers: metabolic evaluation including 24-hour urine, guided by stone analysis.
Hypercalciuria: thiazide and/or alkaline citrate. Hyperuricosuria: allopurinol. Hypocitraturia: alkaline citrate or sodium bicarbonate (EAU).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Calling it renal colic in an older patient without excluding a leaking aortic aneurysm.
Discharging a patient with an obstructing stone and fever; this needs decompression, not just antibiotics.
Relying on opioids or antispasmodics instead of NSAIDs.
Advising a low-calcium diet, which increases stone risk.
Not confirming stone passage, leaving silent obstruction and loss of renal function.

drugs.name: Diclofenac
drugs.dose: 75 mg deep IM once for acute colic; then 100 to 150 mg a day orally or rectally in divided doses for 3 to 10 days (maximum 150 mg a day)
drugs.notes: Avoid in CKD, heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, GI bleeding risk and late pregnancy.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen
drugs.dose: 400 to 600 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours (maximum 2.4 g a day)

drugs.name: Paracetamol (IV)
drugs.dose: 1 g IV every 6 hours if over 50 kg; 15 mg/kg if 50 kg or less (maximum 4 g a day, or 60 mg/kg a day)
drugs.notes: When NSAIDs are contraindicated or insufficient.

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.dose: IV in small titrated increments (about 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg) to effect
drugs.notes: Only after NSAIDs and IV paracetamol fail or are contraindicated. Avoid pethidine. Reduce dose in the elderly and in CKD.

drugs.name: Tamsulosin (MET)
drugs.dose: 400 micrograms orally once daily for up to about 4 weeks
drugs.notes: Off-label. Distal ureteric stones 5 to 10 mm. Postural hypotension.

drugs.name: Alkaline citrate (potassium citrate)
drugs.dose: 3.25 to 9.75 g a day (10 to 30 mmol a day) orally, titrated to urine pH
drugs.notes: Hypocitraturia, uric acid dissolution and prevention. Caution with hyperkalaemia and CKD.

drugs.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
drugs.notes: Hypercalciuria. Hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia; advise regular skin checks (skin cancer risk).
